passages.evidence:
The circuit structure is adapted from Aksay et al. (2007), with tuning and noise assumptions adjusted to primate evidence. Its weights are fitted so that a range of commands can persist in the mean-rate model. This is different from fitting an eye-drift trace.

The spikes are more regular than a Poisson process. The model generates candidate events at $M$ times the desired rate and retains every $M$th event. At constant rate, each retained interval sums $M$ exponential waiting times, giving interval coefficient of variation $1/\sqrt M$. This preserves the mean firing rate while reducing interval variability. The published simulations use integrator variability around 0.22 and motor-neuron variability around 0.07.

Simulating the random events requires a rule for generating repeatable sample sequences. A [[**random seed**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} fixes the starting state of a pseudorandom generator so that a specified implementation can repeat its sample sequence.]{.definition-explanation} The seed controls which sequence is drawn; it does not set the intended firing-rate distribution. The code uses a trajectory index to choose that starting state.

::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Published parameters and public-code settings have different sources"}

The final main Methods report an integrator size $N=30{,}000$, 1,000 motor neurons, synaptic time constant 20 ms, and feedback strength $A=0.015$. The feedback delay is about 70 ms. These are the main model settings, not values to combine with the different comparison runs in the supplement.

The inspected MATLAB code sets its internal update interval to $10^{-5}$ s and saves every 100 steps, giving 1 ms output samples. It uses a 10 ms motor-neuron synaptic time constant, initializes central gaze, and sets the random seed from the trajectory index. Synaptic decay is updated by first-order Euler steps. The mechanical calculation updates velocity and then position.

The code's `N` creates a vector in each of the paired populations, whereas the paper describes $N$ as the network's neuron number. That convention must be resolved before claiming a function call reproduces the published size. The code also uses a different motor-neuron variability regression from the final printed Eq. 35.[^simeye-code]

NumPy's `Generator` supplies random samples for a Python implementation. To repeat a sequence using a [random seed](ch-simulating-eye.html#sec-simulating-eye-path), record the generator, software versions, and order of calls as well as the seed. A seed alone does not guarantee identical results after changing the program or library version.[^simtools-numpy]

SciPy's `solve_ivp` integrates ordinary differential equations from an initial state. It can handle deterministic decay or a deterministic rate model. A stochastic spiking model also needs rules for generating events and applying their jumps. A Brownian-noise model needs a numerical method with the appropriate random increments. Passing freshly drawn noise into an adaptive deterministic solver does not, by itself, specify either model.[^simtools-ode]

answers.claim: A seed chooses a pseudorandom generator starting state, allowing a specified implementation to repeat the sample sequence.
answers.reason: This preserves the baseline definition while moving it before the concrete seed setting. It identifies what acts on what: the seed initializes generator state, which selects a generated sample sequence. It does not promise cross-version or changed-program identity.

answers.claim: The seed chooses the sequence, not the intended firing-rate distribution; the code uses trajectory index for the seed.
answers.reason: The stochastic model and rate rule determine the intended event law. Initialization selects its realization. Individual sampled trajectories and their realized rates can differ without changing that intended model. The trajectory-index statement repeats the already checked baseline setting, adding no new API or statistical guarantee.
